In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the electronic structure of Yb atoms and the development of a compact optical atomic clock.
the development of optical frequency standards based on the clock transition in Yb atoms.
the measurement of the hyperfine splitting and quenching of the 171Yb optical clock transition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 1.4 GHz clock transition in (171)Lu is the most accurate frequency standard in existence today.
the hyperfine quarkonium-quarkonium-quark coupling constant has been measured in the quarkonium-quarks.
the 6s2(1)S0(1/2) → 6s6 p(3)P0(1/1/2) clock transition is a good candidate for an optical frequency standard.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have determined the hyperfine quashing rate in free Yb and the hyperfine splitting in solid Ne.
we have demonstrated a new method for measuring hyperfine quench rates of atomic levels and that the method is applicable to any atomic species.
we have measured the (3)S(0) - (3)P (0,1) transition rates in (171) Yb, and we have also measured the hyperfine quashing rate for (3)P0.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the (3)S(0) - (3)P (0) hyperfine transition in (171)(Yb) has a very small natural linewidth of 1.2 Hz, which is an important property for realizing a high-performance optical clock based on Yb atoms.
the hyperfine quencing rate of (171)YB is much larger than that of (171)Tm, and this difference can be attributed to the different electronic structure of the two atoms.
the (3)D(1) state is not a dominant quencher of the clock transition.
